label: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior
claim: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.
quote: if one ignores the need for analysis and instead just looks at the results of computer experiments, then one quickly finds that even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior.
scope: simple iterative systems defined by arithmetic operations on numbers
measurable_quantities: digit-sequence patterns of iterated values
statistical randomness of iterated values
presence or absence of repetition
candidate_data: Reproducible by direct computation in any arbitrary-precision arithmetic environment; integer sequences in the OEIS.

label: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior
claim: Systems based on numbers that traditional mathematics (e.g. calculus) can analyze completely end up showing only fairly simple behavior; textbook systems are selected for analyzability and therefore are simple.
quote: Inevitably, however, when such complete analysis is possible, the final behavior that is found is fairly simple.
scope: number-based systems treated in traditional science and mathematics
candidate_data: none known

label: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure
claim: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.
quote: Some small-scale structure is visible, but on a larger scale the pattern seems for all practical purposes random.
scope: base-2 digit sequences of powers of 3
measurable_quantities: statistical randomness tests on base-2 digits of 3^n
frequency of digit blocks
candidate_data: Directly computable with arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic; OEIS lists powers of 3.

label: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random
claim: The fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2, a base-independent measure of size, show the same complexity and apparent randomness that appears in their digit sequences.
quote: they too exhibit the kind of complexity and apparent randomness that is evident at the level of digits.
scope: fractional parts of (3/2)^n
measurable_quantities: distribution of fractional parts of (3/2)^n
correlations between successive values
candidate_data: Directly computable with exact rational arithmetic; there is extensive number-theory literature on the distribution of (3/2)^n mod 1.

label: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits
claim: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.
quote: So even if one just looks at overall sizes of whole numbers it is still possible to get great complexity in systems based on numbers.
scope: simple piecewise arithmetic maps on whole numbers
measurable_quantities: sizes of iterated values over millions of steps
detection of eventual periodicity
statistics of size fluctuations
candidate_data: Directly computable with arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic.

label: Non-local arithmetic rules still behave like local cellular automata
claim: Although arithmetic operations are non-local in digits (carries can propagate arbitrarily far) while cellular automaton rules are local, the overall behavior of number-based systems is very similar to that of cellular automata, so the details of underlying rules do not crucially affect the kinds of behavior that occur.
quote: But despite fundamental differences like this in underlying rules, the overall behavior produced by systems based on numbers is still very similar to what one sees for example in cellular automata.
scope: number-based systems compared with cellular automata and other simple programs
measurable_quantities: classification of behavior types (repetitive, nested, random, localized structures) across rule families
candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating simple arithmetic and cellular automaton rules.

label: Reverse-and-add in base 2 shows localized structures and never repeats
claim: The base-2 reverse-and-add process (add a number to its digit-reversal) started from 512 produces localized structures like those in cellular automata, and its overall pattern never appears to become simply repetitive.
quote: Localized structures are visible, but the overall pattern never seems to take on any kind of simple repetitive form.
scope: base-2 reverse-and-add iteration from particular starting numbers
measurable_quantities: digit patterns over millions of steps
detection of eventual periodic structure
candidate_data: Directly computable with arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic; OEIS contains base-2 reverse-and-add trajectories.

label: Recursive sequences using only addition and subtraction can be complex
claim: Recursive integer sequences whose rule refers back a variable distance (e.g. f[n - f[n - 1]]) and uses only addition and subtraction can produce fluctuations that are complex and in many respects random.
quote: even though the rules ultimately involve only addition and subtraction, they nevertheless correspond to programs that are capable of producing behavior of great complexity.
scope: nested recursive integer sequences (Hofstadter-like sequences)
measurable_quantities: fluctuations of f[n] about its trend
balance of positive and negative fluctuations
correlation with base-2 digits of n
candidate_data: OEIS entries for Hofstadter-type meta-Fibonacci sequences, and direct computation.

label: The sequence of primes is in many respects random
claim: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.
quote: the actual sequence of primes that is obtained seems in many respects remarkably random.
scope: the sequence of prime numbers
measurable_quantities: prime gaps
deviations of prime counts from Li(x)
parity of number of primes below n
randomness tests on prime indicator sequence
candidate_data: OEIS prime sequences and gap records, published prime tables, and fast sieving software such as primesieve.

label: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules
claim: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.
quote: such sequences of numbers exhibit complexity that somehow arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules by which the sequences are generated.
scope: integer sequences defined by simple number-theoretic properties
measurable_quantities: randomness statistics of divisor-function and representation-count sequences
candidate_data: OEIS entries for divisor sums, sum-of-squares counts and Goldbach partition counts.

label: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes
claim: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.
quote: Despite the simplicity of its definition, the digit sequence of π seems for practical purposes completely random.
scope: digit sequence of pi in any base
measurable_quantities: digit and block frequencies of pi
statistical randomness test results on pi's digits
candidate_data: Published large-scale computations of pi's digits (trillions of digits) and statistical normality analyses of them.

label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
claim: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.
quote: In fact, rational numbers turn out to be the only kinds of numbers that have repetitive digit sequences.
scope: digit expansions of real numbers
candidate_data: Standard proofs in elementary number theory.

label: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits
claim: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.
quote: so far as one can tell, all whole numbers other than perfect squares have square roots whose digit sequences appear completely random.
scope: digit sequences of square roots of non-square integers
measurable_quantities: digit and block frequencies of square roots
statistical randomness tests on their digits
candidate_data: Published high-precision digit computations of sqrt(2) and other square roots, and direct computation.

label: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits
claim: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
quote: And so far as one can tell, almost all these kinds of numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
scope: digit sequences of higher roots, logarithms and exponentials of small integers
measurable_quantities: digit and block frequencies
statistical randomness tests on digit expansions
candidate_data: Published high-precision computations of constants such as e, log 2 and cube roots, and direct computation.

label: Roots never have nested digit sequences
claim: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).
quote: such a digit sequence never corresponds to a number that can be obtained by the mathematical operation of taking roots.
scope: digit expansions of algebraic numbers obtained as roots
candidate_data: Published transcendence results on automatic (substitution-generated) numbers in the number-theory literature.

label: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random
claim: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.
quote: But for π, as well as for cube roots, fourth roots, and so on, the continued fraction representations one gets seem essentially random.
scope: continued fraction expansions of common irrational numbers
measurable_quantities: distribution of continued fraction terms compared with the Gauss–Kuzmin distribution
periodicity of terms
candidate_data: OEIS entries for continued fraction terms of pi, cube roots and e, and direct computation.

label: Numbers from simple operations are intrinsically complex in any representation
claim: For any representation of numbers in which recovering the value takes comparable effort for all numbers, some numbers look simple but others produced by simple mathematical operations look random, so such numbers are often intrinsically complex independent of representation.
quote: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations are often in some intrinsic sense complex, independent of the particular representation that one uses to look at them.
scope: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations, across number representations
measurable_quantities: apparent randomness of the same numbers across digit, continued-fraction and other representations
candidate_data: Directly computable for standard representations; none known for a general test.

label: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
claim: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.
quote: for any curve like Sin[x] + Sin[α x] the relative arrangements of these crossing points turn out to be related to the output of a generalized substitution system in which the rule at each step is obtained from a term in the continued fraction representation of (α - 1)/(α + 1).
scope: zero sets of sums of two sinusoids
measurable_quantities: positions of zeros of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] compared with substitution-system output
candidate_data: Directly computable numerically; related results in the literature on Sturmian sequences.

label: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition
claim: The shift map (doubling modulo 1) generates no randomness of its own: it just moves digits of the initial number leftward, so its output is random only if the initial number's digit sequence was already random.
quote: in no real sense is any randomness actually being generated by the evolution of this system. Instead, it is just that randomness that was inserted in the digit sequence of the original number shows up in the results one gets.
scope: the shift map and similar chaotic maps that act as digit shifts
measurable_quantities: outputs of the shift map from initial conditions with simple versus random digit sequences
candidate_data: Directly computable with exact rational or arbitrary-precision arithmetic.

label: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds
claim: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.
quote: a crucial discovery in this book is that systems like (a) and (b) on pages 150 and 151 can show behavior that seems in many respects random even when their initial conditions show no sign of randomness and are in fact extremely simple.
scope: simple one-dimensional iterated maps on [0, 1]
measurable_quantities: randomness statistics of iterates from rational initial conditions
digit-sequence complexity of iterates
candidate_data: Directly computable with exact rational arithmetic.

label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness
claim: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.
quote: this phenomenon on its own can make no contribution at all to what we can reasonably consider the ultimate production of randomness.
scope: chaotic dynamical systems and iterated maps
candidate_data: none known

label: Continuous cellular automata show the same complexity as discrete ones
claim: Cellular automata whose cells take a continuous range of gray levels, updated by simple maps of the neighborhood average, show the same kind of complexity as ordinary discrete cellular automata, and can even show localized structures.
quote: despite the presence of continuous gray levels, the behavior that is produced exhibits the same kind of complexity that we have seen in many ordinary cellular automata and other systems with discrete underlying elements.
scope: one-dimensional continuous-valued cellular automata
measurable_quantities: spatial-temporal patterns of gray levels
randomness statistics
presence of localized structures
candidate_data: Directly computable with exact or high-precision arithmetic.

label: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident
claim: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.
quote: I suspect that in fact the current predominance of partial differential equations is in many respects a historical accident—and that had computer technology been developed earlier in the history of mathematics, the situation would probably now be very different.
scope: history of mathematical modeling in physics and other sciences
candidate_data: none known

label: Nature does not fundamentally follow continuous differential equations
claim: Although almost all traditional models in physics (Maxwell, Einstein, Schrödinger equations) are partial differential equations, nature does not fundamentally follow these continuous mathematical abstractions.
quote: it is certainly not that nature fundamentally follows these abstractions.
scope: fundamental laws of physics
candidate_data: none known

label: Simple partial differential equations can show complex behavior
claim: Complex behavior of the kind seen in simple programs is not restricted to discrete systems: some fairly simple partial differential equations, found by searching, produce highly complex patterns, even with apparently discrete patches.
quote: we now know that the same kind of behavior can also occur in completely continuous systems such as partial differential equations.
scope: one-dimensional nonlinear partial differential equations
measurable_quantities: numerical solutions of the equations
robustness of patterns across numerical schemes and resolutions
candidate_data: Reproducible by numerical PDE solvers.

label: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect
claim: Complexity is probably not fundamentally rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones; it was much easier to discover in discrete systems because they can be studied directly by computer experiment without approximation artifacts.
quote: Probably complexity is not in any fundamental sense rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones. But the point is that discrete systems can typically be investigated in a much more direct way than continuous ones.
scope: continuous versus discrete dynamical systems
measurable_quantities: fraction of sampled rules showing complex behavior in continuous versus discrete rule spaces
candidate_data: none known

label: Phenomena seen in discrete simple programs also occur in simple continuous systems
claim: Essentially all of the phenomena observed in discrete simple programs can also be found in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
quote: I suspect that essentially all of the various phenomena that we have observed in discrete systems in the past several chapters can in fact also be found even in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
scope: continuous systems such as continuous cellular automata, iterated maps and partial differential equations
measurable_quantities: occurrence of repetitive, nested, random and localized-structure behavior in continuous rule families
candidate_data: none known

label: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity
claim: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.
quote: adding more dimensions does not ultimately seem to have much effect on the occurrence of behavior of any significant complexity.
scope: simple programs (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems) in one, two and three dimensions
measurable_quantities: fraction of rules showing complex behavior by dimension
classes of behavior by dimension
candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating cellular automaton and Turing machine rules in several dimensions.

label: Slices of 2D cellular automata resemble 1D cellular automata
claim: The complexity inside patterns generated by two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata is very similar to that of one-dimensional cellular automata: a one-dimensional slice through the 2D pattern evolves much like an ordinary 1D cellular automaton.
quote: if one looks at the evolution of a one-dimensional slice through each two-dimensional pattern the results one gets are strikingly similar to what we have seen in ordinary one-dimensional cellular automata.
scope: two-dimensional outer totalistic cellular automata from a single seed
measurable_quantities: space-time patterns of central slices
comparison with 1D elementary cellular automaton classes
candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

label: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles
claim: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.
quote: it is even possible to find cellular automata that yield overall shapes that closely approximate perfect circles.
scope: two-dimensional outer totalistic cellular automata with 8 neighbors
measurable_quantities: deviation of pattern boundary from a circle
growth rate of radius with steps
candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

label: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors
claim: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.
quote: there can be great complexity not only in the detailed arrangement of black and white cells in a two-dimensional cellular automaton pattern, but also in the overall shape of the pattern.
scope: two-dimensional growth-type cellular automata
measurable_quantities: boundary shape of growing patterns over time
whether growth stops
candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

label: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior
claim: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.
quote: But overall it seems that the basic kinds of behavior produced are just the same as in one and two dimensions.
scope: three-dimensional cellular automata
measurable_quantities: classes of behavior across sampled 3D rules
candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

label: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D
claim: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).
quote: For Turing machines with two or three possible states, only repetitive and nested behavior normally seem to occur. With four states, more complex behavior is possible, but it is still rather rare.
scope: two-dimensional Turing machines with two to four head states and two colors
measurable_quantities: fraction of enumerated or randomly sampled rules showing non-nested behavior
candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating or sampling two-dimensional Turing machine rules.

label: Neighbor-independent geometric replacement rules always give nested fractals
claim: Substitution systems and geometric replacement rules in which each element is replaced independently of other elements, including those of traditional fractal geometry, inevitably produce purely nested patterns.
quote: with this kind of setup, it is ultimately inevitable that all the patterns produced must have a completely regular nested structure.
scope: neighbor-independent two-dimensional substitution systems and iterated geometric replacement rules
candidate_data: Standard results on self-similar sets and iterated function systems.

label: Fractal geometry misses complexity by excluding interactions between elements
claim: Traditional fractal geometry does not consider interactions between elements, which is why all patterns it produces are purely nested; allowing replacements to depend on neighbors on a grid readily yields complicated, non-nested patterns.
quote: in traditional fractal geometry the idea of interaction between elements is not considered—so that all patterns that are produced have a purely nested form.
scope: fractal geometry and two-dimensional neighbor-dependent substitution systems
candidate_data: none known

label: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension
claim: Networks in which every node is identical and has exactly two outgoing connections can, purely by the pattern of connections, form structures equivalent to arrays of any number of dimensions, as well as trees and nested structures.
quote: using the same principles an array with any number of dimensions can easily be obtained.
scope: directed networks with out-degree two
candidate_data: Constructive proof by explicit network construction.

label: Network rules depending on distance-two neighborhoods can give random growth
claim: Network systems whose rewiring rules depend only on whether a node's two connections lead to the same node always grow in an essentially repetitive way, but when rules depend on nodes up to two connections away, even the number of nodes can vary in an apparently random way (in about one in 10,000 rules).
quote: even the total number of nodes at each step can vary in a way that seems in many respects completely random.
scope: network systems with local rewiring and node-insertion rules
measurable_quantities: node count per step
fraction of sampled rules with non-repetitive node counts
candidate_data: Directly computable by simulating network rewriting rules.

label: Network systems may underlie the structure of space and spacetime
claim: Some network systems will likely turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
quote: I suspect that some of these systems will in the end turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
scope: fundamental structure of physical space and spacetime
candidate_data: none known

label: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all
claim: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.
quote: most either grow exponentially quickly, or not at all; slow growth of the kind seen on the facing page is rather rare.
scope: multiway (non-deterministic string rewriting) systems with simple rules
measurable_quantities: number of distinct states per step across enumerated rules
growth-rate classification
candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating simple string rewriting rules.

label: Slowly growing multiway systems eventually become repetitive
claim: Even when slowly growing multiway systems show early apparent randomness in their state counts, they typically end up showing some form of repetition (sometimes with long periods, such as 1071 steps).
quote: even when such growth leads to a certain amount of apparent randomness it typically in the end seems to exhibit some form of repetition.
scope: slowly growing multiway systems
measurable_quantities: state counts per step
detected period of differences in state counts
candidate_data: Directly computable by simulating multiway systems.

label: Multiway systems build their own network of connections in time
claim: Because each sequence in a multiway system always leads to the same successors, the evolution can be represented as a network of which state leads to which, so multiway systems build up their own, often complicated, pattern of connections in time.
quote: multiway systems can in effect build up their own pattern of connections in time—and this pattern can often be quite complicated.
scope: multiway systems
candidate_data: none known

label: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern
claim: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.
quote: in one dimension it is possible to prove that any local set of constraints that can be satisfied at all can always be satisfied by some simple and purely repetitive arrangement of colors.
scope: one-dimensional local constraint systems (one-dimensional subshifts of finite type)
candidate_data: Standard results in symbolic dynamics.

label: All satisfiable 2D nearest-neighbor template constraints allow repetitive patterns
claim: Of all 4,294,967,296 two-dimensional constraints defined by allowed templates of a cell and its four neighbors, 766,979,044 cannot be satisfied, and every one of the rest can be satisfied by a repetitive pattern, with 171 repetitive patterns sufficing for all.
quote: among the 3,527,988,252 that remain, it turns out that every single one can be satisfied by a simple repetitive pattern.
scope: two-dimensional two-color constraints on five-cell (von Neumann) neighborhood templates
measurable_quantities: count of unsatisfiable constraint sets
number of distinct repetitive patterns needed
candidate_data: Reproducible by exhaustive computer search with tiling and SAT-solver tools.

label: Constraint systems require going outside the system to find their patterns
claim: Unlike rule-based systems, which can be run directly, systems defined by constraints offer no direct procedure for finding the patterns they allow; one must search from outside the system, which can take enormous computational effort.
quote: But in a system that is based on constraints, there is no such direct procedure, and instead one must in effect always go outside of the system to work out what patterns can occur.
scope: systems defined by constraints versus explicit evolution rules
candidate_data: none known

label: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one
claim: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.
quote: after examining more than 18 million of them, one finally discovers the system shown on the facing page. And in this system, unlike all others before it, no repetitive pattern is possible; the only pattern that satisfies the constraint is the non-repetitive nested pattern shown in the picture.
scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition
measurable_quantities: position in enumeration of first constraint forcing non-periodicity
structure of the forced pattern
candidate_data: Reproducible by computer search; related literature on aperiodic tilings and Wang tiles.

label: No tested simple template constraint forces more than nested behavior
claim: Of the 137,438,953,472 template constraints with a required-template condition, none of the millions tested forces anything more complicated than nested behavior.
quote: of the millions of these that I have tested, none have forced anything more complicated than the kind of nested behavior seen on the previous page.
scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition
measurable_quantities: fraction of tested constraints forcing non-repetitive, nested or more complex patterns
candidate_data: Reproducible by computer search with SAT solvers.

label: 3x3 template constraints can force a rule 30–like random pattern
claim: Constraints on 3×3 blocks of cells can be constructed to force complex patterns: a set of 56 allowed templates forces a unique, largely random pattern equivalent to the evolution of the rule 30 cellular automaton.
quote: a system with 56 allowed templates in which the only pattern satisfying the constraint is a complex and largely random one, derived from the rule 30 cellular automaton.
scope: two-dimensional constraints on 3×3 neighborhoods
candidate_data: Verifiable by explicit construction and SAT-based checking.

label: Simple constraints rarely force complex behavior, unlike simple rules
claim: Unlike simple evolution rules, almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns; complex behavior forced by constraints is rare.
quote: it seems that almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns.
scope: constraint-based systems compared with rule-based simple programs
measurable_quantities: fraction of constraint sets forcing non-repetitive patterns versus fraction of rules producing complex behavior
candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating constraint systems and cellular automaton rules.

label: Constraint-like equations helped hide complexity from traditional science
claim: Because describing complex behavior with constraints requires fairly complicated constraints, the traditional focus of science and mathematics on equations that act like constraints is another reason they failed to identify the phenomenon of complexity.
quote: the fact that traditional science and mathematics tends to concentrate on equations that operate like constraints provides yet another reason for their failure to identify the fundamental phenomenon of complexity that I discuss in this book.
scope: methods of traditional science and mathematics
candidate_data: none known
